network.tdh.formal.metadataDescription: TDH-v1 as a Lean 4 model: what it reproduces, what its proofs establish, what turned out to be false, and what the proofs do not cover.
network.tdh.formal.title: Formal model
network.tdh.formal.lede: TDH-v1 is also written as a mathematical model in Lean 4, a language in which a computer checks every step of every proof. The model runs, so it computes real days of TDH, and it carries proofs of the rule’s key properties. This page says what is proved, what was shown false, and what the proofs do not cover.
network.tdh.formal.status: A proposal, not yet adopted. The English specification, P26, stays the rule; the plan is for this model to become the normative reference for the computation.
network.tdh.formal.build: Results of {date}: Lean {version}, model at commit {commit} of 6529’s design repository, following P26 as clarified at {spec}. Source to be published.

network.tdh.formal.summary.falseBody: Each with a counterexample the build checks, and each now reflected in P26
network.tdh.formal.summary.vectorsBody: {checks} checks, the same count as the Rust implementation

network.tdh.formal.why.title: Why write the rule again
network.tdh.formal.why.body: Plain English can be read more than one way. When a second implementation was written from the specification alone, it recorded 23 places where it had to make a choice. Two were rated high: whether N in the boost means the day number or the count of Memes, which give different boosts, and how to decode the delegation events at all, since P26 then gave no layouts. P26 now states a rule for each.
network.tdh.formal.why.body2: A formal model leaves no such room: every term has exactly one meaning, and the computer rejects a proof with a gap. Writing it paid off. It proved that the first version of D131’s netting rule could be changed by steps inside a transaction, in five cases, after the separately written program B found the flaw; P26’s uniform rule fixes all five. Its questions about P26 led to the clarifications of 15 October, and its proofs showed which claims hold and which do not.
network.tdh.formal.featured.title: One theorem, read two ways
network.tdh.formal.featured.plain: Take two inputs whose transactions correspond one to one: each pair shares one timestamp and one transaction hash, and moves the same net amount of every token for every address. If both replays succeed, with netting and the same consolidations, they leave every holding stack the same, for every token and every address.
network.tdh.formal.featured.means: So the order of a transaction’s steps, its round trips and its detours cannot change any holding stack, and so no balance and no raw days.
network.tdh.formal.featured.limit: It stops there. Mint counts read the logged steps, so a mint and its burn inside one transaction leave every stack unchanged but can change editions, rates and other holders’ TDH (the counterexample below). The underflow test also reads the steps, to decide whether an input is valid.
network.tdh.formal.featured.definitions: Its hypotheses, as defined in the model
network.tdh.formal.figure.title: Two inputs, one net movement
network.tdh.formal.figure.desc: Left: one transaction as logged, with three steps: A sends a copy to X, X sends it back, A sends a copy to B. Right: one transaction with one step, A sends a copy to B. Both move the same net amount for every address: A minus one, B plus one, X zero. Replayed with netting, both leave every holding stack the same.
network.tdh.formal.figure.result: Same holding stacks, balances and raw days
network.tdh.formal.figure.resultNote: A keeps its other copies with their ages; B’s new copy starts at this transaction.
network.tdh.formal.contains.title: What the model contains
network.tdh.formal.contains.body: The model covers P26 from canonical decoded inputs to the day’s records and totals, one module per part of the specification, including the input rules clarified on 15 October and a registry whose every field the rules read. Each definition quotes or cites its P26 section, and P26’s pseudocode sits next to the code that implements it. All arithmetic is on unbounded integers, so nothing can overflow or round by accident; the two binary64 roundings are emulated exactly.
network.tdh.formal.contains.runs: The model runs. It passes all 61 conformance vectors ({checks} checks); it computes the 2026-10-11 cycle from 414,007 raw Ethereum logs, in about {seconds} seconds, with the live total of {total} and all 21,410 wallet and identity records unchanged; and it matched the Python reference on 6,000 random inputs under both netting rules ({randomChecks} checks).
network.tdh.formal.contains.outside: Outside the model: selecting and decoding Ethereum logs, state reads and finality, the binding of the result header, and the legacy emulation. The vector runner has its own log decoder; it is test tooling, not part of the model.
network.tdh.formal.module.caption: Modules of the model
network.tdh.formal.module.basic: Rounding, addresses, ZERO and DEAD; binary64 by exact integer emulation
network.tdh.formal.module.registry: The parameter registry, its constraints and its Keccak-256 hash
network.tdh.formal.module.inputs: Decoded transfers and delegation events, canonical order and log positions (decoding itself is not modelled)
network.tdh.formal.module.cutoff: Cycle day, boundary, snapshot block and header order, whole days
network.tdh.formal.module.eligibility: Eligibility, editions and floors, rates, seasons
network.tdh.formal.module.consolidation: Kept events, pair state, clusters, identity keys
network.tdh.formal.module.holdings: Acquisition stacks, the underflow test, transaction netting, the replay, per-token values
network.tdh.formal.module.arithmetic: RATE, BASE, ADD, the boost in cents, FINAL
network.tdh.formal.module.scores: Boost, records, finals, daily rates, range checks
network.tdh.formal.module.cycle: The whole cycle: records, totals, range checks, output
network.tdh.formal.statements.title: What is proved, and what is not
network.tdh.formal.statements.intro: Every theorem below is checked at every build and audited to use only Lean’s three standard axioms; a proof with a gap fails the build. One statement holds by definition, P26’s stated numbers are checked by running the model, and four claims turned out to be false.
network.tdh.formal.statements.caption: Statements, {shown} of {total} shown
network.tdh.formal.st.netting.title: Netting invariance
network.tdh.formal.st.netting.plain: Every holding stack after the replay depends only on each transaction’s net movement of each token per address. Reordering a transaction’s transfers, or inserting a round trip anywhere in it, through a sink or not, changes no stack, and so no balance and no raw days.
network.tdh.formal.st.netting.scope: Assumes that both replays succeed, that each pair of corresponding transactions shares one timestamp and one transaction hash (P26 §3.2 requires it and the model checks it), and the same consolidations. It does not extend to base, boost or final: mint counts read the logged steps (see “Steps inside a transaction never matter” below).
network.tdh.formal.st.replay.title: The replay never fails
network.tdh.formal.st.replay.plain: Once the underflow test passes, the replay succeeds, with or without netting, and every stack outside the sinks holds exactly its address’s balance: what it received minus what it sent. That is why P26 need not test for underflow again in the replay.
network.tdh.formal.st.replay.scope: With netting, it also assumes P26’s transaction rules (one timestamp and transaction hash, net movements below 2^64). A sink’s stack is not a balance: sinks only receive.
network.tdh.formal.st.conservation.title: Copies are conserved
network.tdh.formal.st.conservation.plain: Summed over every address outside the sinks, the copies held of a token are the copies that came from a sink minus those that went to one. An address that never appears holds none.
network.tdh.formal.st.conservation.scope: The inflow counts transfers from the zero address (mints) and from 0x…dead, which creates copies (P26 §3.4). Holds for any registry’s sinks.
network.tdh.formal.st.identitySums.title: Identity sums
network.tdh.formal.st.identitySums.plain: In every day’s result, each identity’s balance, raw days and base TDH, in total and for every token, are the sums over exactly its wallet records, each counted once; and every wallet record belongs to exactly one identity.
network.tdh.formal.st.identitySums.scope: Not for boost and final, which are computed per record: see “Total = sum of wallets” below.
network.tdh.formal.st.order.title: Order independence
network.tdh.formal.st.order.plain: Reordering the input’s transfers and delegation events in any way gives the same result, or the same error, including the log-position checks of P26 §3.1. The order in which logs arrive cannot matter.
network.tdh.formal.st.order.scope: A transfer’s position fields are part of the input: changing them changes the canonical order, as it should.
network.tdh.formal.st.lifo.title: Last in, first out
network.tdh.formal.st.lifo.plain: The model’s compact stack is exactly P26’s ordered list: a purchase appends, a send removes exactly the last n entries in order and fails exactly when there are fewer, and its size is its length.
network.tdh.formal.st.lifo.scope: Seven theorems about the stack itself.
network.tdh.formal.st.totals.title: Totals
network.tdh.formal.st.totals.plain: The network total is the sum of identity finals, the total without sinks leaves out exactly the sink identities, the base and raw totals are sums too, and the total is below 2^53.
network.tdh.formal.st.totals.scope: This restates how the totals are defined; only the range check adds anything. A sum over wallets is a different number: see “Total = sum of wallets”.
network.tdh.formal.st.facts.title: P26’s stated numbers
network.tdh.formal.st.facts.plain: The registry hash, the half-cent rate ties for H = 3,941, ADD(2) = 50,000, ADD(3) = 82,645, ADD(n) = 144,051 from 33 sets, no ties in the boost’s rounding, and the final ties that round down: 16 checks.
network.tdh.formal.st.facts.scope: Evaluated at every build, which trusts Lean’s compiler; not proved in the kernel.
network.tdh.formal.st.beyondStacks.title: Steps inside a transaction never matter
network.tdh.formal.st.beyondStacks.plain: False beyond the stacks. Inserting a mint of 10 copies and its burn into one transaction leaves every stack unchanged, but 10 more copies count as minted: the largest edition doubles, another card’s rate doubles from 2.00 to 4.00, and another holder’s final doubles from 800 to 1,600.
network.tdh.formal.st.beyondStacks.scope: Counterexample H, checked at every build. P26 §7.1 now states the property for stacks, balances and raw days only. Whether such mints should count toward editions is flagged for the owner, not decided.
network.tdh.formal.st.minted.title: Held = minted − burned
network.tdh.formal.st.minted.plain: False. A transfer from 0x…dead credits its recipient with a fresh copy and is not a mint. Case G: one copy minted, one sent by 0x…dead, two held. What holds instead is the conservation law above.
network.tdh.formal.st.minted.scope: Proved false with a counterexample the build checks.
network.tdh.formal.st.walletSum.title: Total = sum of wallets
network.tdh.formal.st.walletSum.plain: False. Each record’s boost is computed on its own holdings. Case F: two wallets of one identity each hold one Gradient for 100 days; each wallet record has boost 1.02 and final 102, and the identity has boost 1.04 and final 208. The total is 208, not 204.
network.tdh.formal.st.walletSum.scope: P26 §7.3 now says so, with this example. A page that adds up wallet values will not match the total.
network.tdh.formal.st.firstRule.title: The first netting rule
network.tdh.formal.st.firstRule.plain: False: under D131’s first rule, steps inside a transaction could change even the holding stacks. Five cases are proved in the kernel; the uniform rule P26 adopted the same day gives equal results in each.
network.tdh.formal.st.firstRule.scope: Totals from the model, first rule against the current one.
network.tdh.formal.st.cap.title: The 19.99% cap
network.tdh.formal.st.cap.plain: With at least six parties of positive weight, no party, capped or not, counts more than 19.99% of the counted total, and the key slices add up exactly. For the live roster this holds for the registered weight W with no further assumption, because an account is live only while it keeps a valid key. The loop stops within six passes.
network.tdh.formal.st.cap.scope: A separate small model of the cap. Group membership, the lease and key validity are inputs; with fewer than six parties there is no cap and the theorems say nothing.
network.tdh.formal.st.exclusions.title: Exclusions
network.tdh.formal.st.exclusions.plain: For a node that keeps incident records, each with its step and length fixed when it opens, as P53 §13.1 now prescribes: no evidence shortens an exclusion in force, exclusions never overlap, stretch or repeat, and pruning old records on P53’s schedule changes no exclusion.
network.tdh.formal.st.exclusions.scope: For a node that recomputes incidents from the evidence it still holds, the claim is false: an exclusion can end 298 cycles early. P53 now rules recomputation out.
network.tdh.formal.cases.caption: The first netting rule against the current one
network.tdh.formal.cases.desc.A: The order of a pass-through’s two outgoing legs
network.tdh.formal.cases.desc.B: The order of a burn and a forwarded mint
network.tdh.formal.cases.desc.C: Two sends, without and with a round trip appended
network.tdh.formal.cases.desc.D: A round trip placed before a pass-through
network.tdh.formal.cases.desc.E: A mint and a burn inside a pass-through
network.tdh.formal.not.title: What the proofs do not guarantee
network.tdh.formal.not.english.title: That the English text says the same thing.
network.tdh.formal.not.english.body: People check that the model matches the specification; a disagreement is fixed in one or the other and recorded. On 15 October P26 settled the ten questions the model had raised. Three remain open: how two rules apply to inputs given already decoded (header order, and transfers that share one log position), and, flagged for the owner, whether mints inside a transaction should count toward editions.
network.tdh.formal.not.programs.title: That the programs match the model on every input.
network.tdh.formal.not.programs.body: The model, the Python reference and the design repository’s second Rust implementation pass the same 61 vectors, and the model matched the Python reference on a whole real day and on 6,000 random inputs. A differential test on 15 October ran 40,000 generated cycles through the model, the Python reference, the Rust core and program B: they agreed on every value, and differed only on whether 20 inputs were valid, a case P26 has since made explicit (§3.1, vector 51). Tests can miss cases: no machine-checked proof links any program’s code to the model.
network.tdh.formal.not.inputs.title: That the inputs are right.
network.tdh.formal.not.inputs.body: Selecting and decoding Ethereum logs, state reads and finality are outside the model. Validators are to check every block’s events against Ethereum’s block headers (D118), and two separately written programs are being built to prove each day’s result from Ethereum’s history (D119).
network.tdh.formal.not.rule.title: That the rule is the right rule.
network.tdh.formal.not.rule.body: A proof shows the rule does what it says, not that it is fair or wise. Rule changes are owner decisions.
network.tdh.formal.not.lean.title: Lean itself.
network.tdh.formal.not.lean.body: The proofs rely on Lean’s small kernel and its three standard axioms, which the build audits for every theorem. The 16 numeric checks and some counterexamples are evaluations that also trust Lean’s compiler.
network.tdh.formal.layers.title: Three layers of assurance
network.tdh.formal.layers.desc: The English specification is checked against the Lean model by people. Inside the Lean model, the proofs are the only machine-checked links. The model and the programs pass the same 61 vectors, the model was compared with the Python reference on a whole day and on 6,000 random inputs, and all four were run on 40,000 generated cycles. The programs check each other: Rust and Python in the daily comparison, and Rust and program B inside every validator once it runs both. Inputs are checked separately.
network.tdh.formal.layers.programsSub: Rust core, program B, Python reference
network.tdh.formal.layers.vectors: 61 shared vectors; a whole day and 6,000 random inputs against Python; 40,000 generated cycles across four programs
network.tdh.formal.layers.inputsBody: Checked reads (D118) and proofs A and B (D119), outside the model
network.tdh.formal.layers.machine: Machine-checked: the proofs inside the Lean model
network.tdh.formal.layers.human: Checked by people or by tests
network.tdh.formal.check.title: How you will be able to check
network.tdh.formal.check.body: The model lives in 6529’s design repository, beside the specification and its vectors. Once that source is published, anyone with Lean installed can rebuild it, which re-checks every proof and audits its axioms, and run the vectors through it:
network.tdh.formal.check.commands:
lake build
lake exe tdh-vectors ../tdh-reference/vectors   # 61 of 61, 1,094 checks
lake exe tdh-vectors vectors-netting           # 4 of 4
